tests.description: Stable direct JIT loads for editable 16/32/64-bit constants, idle capture gate and ring semantics, and executable x64 JIT copies, constant shifts, narrow masks and register flow with physical registers, partial writes, memory operands, flags, prefix fallback and branch relocation checks.

The loader's side of TC_SERVICE_IO_VALUE: the expression parser a value field's text has to survive (0x/0b/0o, ~ - * / % + - << >> & ^ |, parentheses, digit separators), the width truncation every field applies, and the service table's shape.
The punch tape follows the panel it is drawn in: whole byte groups wrap first, then the chips scale into the free box (up on a big window, down on a short drawer) and every bit stays inside the grid.
Build every product, fixture and example, then run the compiled unit/model tests.

The built-in Keyboard component's outputs in the real game, with the loader's generated-program rewrite (src/keyboard_fix.hpp). A board carrying one 0x5d Keyboard - its read strobe driven by a level input the sandbox cannot resolve, which is what makes the game emit the constant-zero strobe - is entered as the sandbox level's board without dev.sandbox-sim, so the game's own JIT program is what runs. tests/keyboard-fix-driver.cpp pushes a key-down and a key-up into the component's own ring buffer (entry down|key<<8, stride 8, wrap 4096, write index at +4098 - the layout simulator_queue_key_down/_up and the level script's add_keyboard_value share), asks the game's sim.do to run, and reads the component's output slots out of the simulation state. Asserted: out1=1 out2=0x41 after the key-down and out1=0 out2=0x41 after the key-up, i.e. the key state and the key code reach the pins; the compiled program (dumped to native-logic-source-keyboard-<n>.txt) reads an undriven strobe unconditionally; and the game's own emission is kept in native-logic-source-<n>.txt for comparison. The -Disabled control run asserts the defect the rewrite removes: with the same board and the same injected events the game's untouched program reports out0=1 (an event is waiting) with out1=0 out2=0x0, because the read never happens and the else branch clears the outputs.

The negative control for keyboard-fix: the identical board and the identical injected key events, run with TC_MODLOADER_KEYBOARD_FIX=0 so the game's own emission is compiled. The Keyboard must then report out0=1 with out1=0 and out2=0x0 for both events - the buffer holds them and the component says one is waiting, while the key code and the key state never reach the outputs. That is the player-visible defect the rewrite fixes, so this run fails if the rewrite is applied to the program anyway.
Declarative game profile schema, generated header freshness and symbol catalogue coverage.
Compile and compare all public C ABI sizes, alignments, offsets and constants.
WordWatchee 64: the value_size clamp in the pinned executable and the shader's 33..64 bit digit extraction.

Save import, path isolation, reparse-point rejection, and the profile management and dependency report the 存档 page drives. The case imports the vanilla save twice in an isolated home (complete copy including Unicode names and binary schematics, cloud metadata excluded, previous imports and the default profile untouched), rejects a linked source and a traversal profile without changing the selection, and then exercises the management core the page and 'tcmod-cli saves ...' share: list reports the selected profile as running, create makes a fresh local- profile and selects it without disturbing the others, duplicate carries the source contents into a copy-, rename moves it, remove moves it into a trash- profile whose contents survive, and removing the profile the next start would use is refused with the selection left alone. It then frames a literal-only Snappy circuit by hand (the encoding tests/float-fixture.cpp writes) holding one custom_id the registry cache knows and one it does not, and requires 'saves report' to name the Mod and type from the cache, to report the unknown type by its author tag, to count both as missing while nothing provides them, and to report nothing for a profile without custom components.
Deterministic Mod archives and declarative release manifest contract.
Native plugin loading, tamper detection, raw-hook conflict and disable behavior.

tc.mod.storage V2 + tc.mod.settings V1 in the real game: a probe migrates global/profile counters to schema 1, registers one global bool and one profile text field during tc_mod_load, then three starts switch A -> B -> A and must report 1/1, 2/1, 3/2. The log must also expose the single host settings page. This proves migration-time availability, persistence/isolation, declarative registration and GLOBAL/PROFILE grouping.
Loader-owned chains, event bus and crash attribution against the offline host.
Install, upgrade, uninstall and incompatible-build rejection.
Identify the pinned executable and original engine against the supported game profile.
Circuit definition import through the real game.
The shipped circuit-and example registers cleanly in the real game.
The byte-adder example passes the stock level in cycle and refresh phases.

Place a component through the real component menu path, then edit the board through the V2 command bus in one isolated sandbox: a placement command (V3/V4 readback finds the new instance), two placements staged in one V2 transaction (staged=2 completed=2, both cells hit), one undo that reverts exactly one step and a redo that restores it, and the delete command built on the game's own undo-aware try_delete - the component disappears, one board.undo puts it back at the same cell and redo removes it again, which the low-level tombstone entry cannot do. The delete's ownership rule is checked with a second package in the sandbox (local.editor-demo): naming another Mod's type is refused before queueing (submit=-2, request untouched, the peer component still on the board) while naming an unregistered type queues and fails with NOT_FOUND.

The internal-netlist builder (tc.component.compose V2, M4's second cut): a probe registers a composite type - a three-input AND built from two of the game's own AND parts - through begin/node/connect/commit, and the game is asked about it twice. Its own prototype read shows the declared pins plus the gate count the game recomputed from the inner nodes (2, while the probe declared 1) and the declared delay; the catalogue shows implementation=COMPOSITE. The same type then sits on the build/nl_and3board.data fixture board of the and_gate_3 level, whose own test drives the three inputs and judges the output - verdict=1 only if the composite's truth table is right. The run also nests one composite inside another and requires a netlist with an undriven input to be refused with a readable reason before anything is imported.

tc.component.editor V4 registration and the description rule: examples/editor-demo installs, the loader registers its 0-pin types, accepts the richer field table ('Component editor V4: type 0x454449545f303031 edits enabled(bool), period(uint), mode(enum), gain(float), mask(uint), label(text), scale(float), format(enum), color(color-rgba8), palette(color-rgba8), preview(custom)') and the V4 staged table ('Component editor V4: type 0x454449545f303033 edits active(bool), count(uint), channel(enum) table=confirm'), and reports both halves of the description default - the settings type keeps its description out of the game's panel, the long type opts in with TC_COMPONENT_TYPE_SHOW_DESCRIPTION and gets it shown.

The host's property rows with real input: tests/component-editor-driver.cpp enters the sandbox, places one editor-demo component through the command bus, clicks its body so the game opens its own drawer, reads the row rectangles the loader logs (TC_EDITOR_TRACE=1) and clicks the 'enabled' checkbox. Asserted: the loader drew a rectangle for that row, the host committed the click through tc.component.storage ('Component editor: committed field enabled'), no write was refused, and the type's own on_config_changed reported the new value (enabled=0 where the registered default is 1).

The same row gate for a text field: the click has to focus the host's InputText (the loader's own trace reports active=1 focused=1 for that row), the typed characters have to land in the instance's configuration bytes and Enter has to commit them - asserted through the type's on_config_changed line carrying the typed text in the label value and the loader's 'committed field label' line.

The radio form of an enum (tc.component.editor V2, TC_COMPONENT_FIELD_RADIO): the row is drawn as one radio button per choice across the panel - the shape examples/float-ops draws by hand today - and the loader's own rectangle for the row is the last choice's button, so clicking there has to commit that choice. Asserted: 'committed field format ... value=Float' plus the type's on_config_changed line reporting format=Float.

The dropdown enum (tc.component.editor V3, TC_COMPONENT_FIELD_DROPDOWN): the row opens a real combo and the entry clicked in its popup is committed. The driver clicks the row, waits one frame for the popup, then clicks the entry - retrying on a different point until the log carries the commit, because ImGui decides where the popup lands. Choice 1 also makes the example's validator warn, so the run asserts both 'committed field mode ... value=RTZ' and 'validator warned for field mode'.

Inline validation (tc.component.editor V3, TCComponentEditorValidateV1) on a real input path: the example's validator refuses the last dropdown choice (RNA). Asserted: the host reports 'validator refused field mode ... the demo refuses RNA', no 'committed field mode' line appears at all, and therefore the instance's configuration keeps the bytes it had.

A custom row (tc.component.editor V3, TC_COMPONENT_FIELD_CUSTOM) with a double click: the host gives the Mod a clipped canvas, its own painted area and the interaction, and the action callback receives TC_COMPONENT_EDITOR_ACTION_DOUBLE_CLICK. Asserted through the example Mod's own action log ('custom action kind=2').

A custom row's context menu (tc.component.editor V3): right-clicking the canvas opens the entries the type declared, and picking one delivers TC_COMPONENT_EDITOR_ACTION_MENU with that action id. Asserted: 'custom action kind=1 id=1' plus the configuration change the menu entry made through tc.component.storage.

A custom row's resize grip (tc.component.editor V3, TC_COMPONENT_FIELD_RESIZE_HANDLE): the host opens one storage edit when the grip is pressed, delivers RESIZE_BEGIN/.../RESIZE_END with the accumulated delta, and commits the span as one undo step. Asserted: all three action kinds reach the Mod and the dragged size lands in the instance's configuration.

The RGBA8 colour row (tc.component.editor V3, TC_COMPONENT_FIELD_COLOR_RGBA8): the field is ImGui's own colour widget, and dragging across it commits the packed 0xAABBGGRR value through the same storage path as every other row. Asserted: 'committed field color' and a stored value that differs from the registered default.

The editor inside the game's own bottom panel, and what happens when that panel is folded: every rows case asserts the loader's row window and the clicked row stay inside the panel rectangle the same trace publishes. This case types into a text row without committing, clicks the game's own fold switch in the drawer's title row, waits ~2.5 s (a still-drawing editor would have traced rows in that window), unfolds it, and requires the rows to come back at the same rectangle with the typed text still in the field before Enter commits it.

The editable hexadecimal widget (V2, TC_COMPONENT_FIELD_HEX): the row is a text box holding the value as 0x-padded hex, the characters the driver types are inserted at the caret the click left behind (editing keys never reach the widget on this build) and Enter commits them. Asserted: the loader's committed value for mask carries the typed digits wherever the caret put them ('0xbeef0010' is the compact-row answer for 'beef'), and the type's on_config_changed line carries the same digits.

A table taller than the screen (32 rows, the field ceiling): the host has to cap its row window at the screen and let ImGui scroll it, or the lower rows would be drawn where nothing can click them. Asserted: the loader's own window trace reports rows=32 with a scroll range above zero, and the first row still takes a click and commits ('f0=0 ... ones=31' on the type's on_config_changed line).

The swatch strip (tc.component.editor V4, TC_COMPONENT_FIELD_COLOR_PALETTE): a colour row whose choices carry colour literals instead of enum labels, drawn as presets the player clicks. The host publishes each swatch's own rectangle, so the driver clicks the one the host drew rather than a fraction of the row. Asserted: the loader published the strip's swatches, 'committed field palette ... value=#...' and the stored word is exactly the clicked preset's packed colour (0xff40e0ff for the third preset, #ffe040).

The editable colour box (tc.component.editor V4, TC_COMPONENT_FIELD_COLOR_HEX): the same row that carries the swatch strip also carries a text box holding the packed 0xAABBGGRR word, the exact-bit escape hatch a colour field otherwise lacks. The driver drags across the box first (the editing keys never reach ImGui on this build, but the mouse does select) and then types, so what lands in the configuration is exactly the typed word rather than whatever the click's caret happened to extend the old one into. Asserted: the loader committed the row and the stored word carries the typed digits.

The one-line validation marker (tc.component.editor V4, TC_COMPONENT_FIELD_VALIDATION_ICON): the message a row is carrying is a small square at the end of its control instead of a line of text under it, and the text itself is readable from the marker's tooltip. The run reuses the refused dropdown choice so the row really is carrying a message, then rests the pointer on the marker. Asserted: the loader published a marker for the mode row with status=-1, the driver aimed at that rectangle, and the hover produced 'Component editor: validation tip ... field="mode" status=-1 message="the demo refuses RNA"'.

A staged table (tc.component.editor V4, TC_COMPONENT_EDITOR_TABLE_CONFIRM): the type's rows land in the host's working copy and nothing reaches the record until Apply. The driver stages the checkbox, picks an enum through its dropdown, and presses Apply. Asserted: both rows report 'staged field', neither reports 'committed field' (a V3 table would write each edit as it happens), the host published its buttons with pending=2, and Apply wrote the batch in one step - 'applied 2 staged field(s) ... in one step' with exactly one on_config_changed line carrying both new values.

The other half of the staged table: Cancel throws the pending edits away. The same two rows are staged and the Cancel button is pressed instead. Asserted: 'cancelled 2 staged field(s)', no 'committed field' for either row, and - the part that matters - no on_config_changed line for the staged type at all, because nothing was ever written.

What a missing Mod costs: the component becomes a tombstone, the file survives until a save, a reinstall restores the configuration, and a save without the Mod loses it.
One Ctrl+Z reverts exactly one configuration commit and one redo re-applies it, driven through the game's own undo entry.
A full 1024-byte configuration (132 record entries) is written, saved and read back, with the schematic growth reported.
Declared gates and timing across the topology regression matrix.
Declarative 8-input/8-output component registration and execution.
Declarative single-pin byte component execution.

A packaged JSON plus .v project registers a five-input V3 RAM and its Chinese responsive in-game source-editor page, captures that page from the real OpenGL framebuffer, materialises an editable per-Mod workspace, preserves a player edit on restart, and reports a broken source with file, line, and component id.

The single-cycle RV32I front end registers through the real game with the exact per-output dependency map: pc-only imem_addr, instr-only rs1/rs2/rd addresses, and the write-back value reading the register file, so the built-in register file no longer forms a false combinational loop.

tc.component.runtime keeps a deleted type in the game's own prototype map, so a file the editor deletes and then recreates with the same name - the same stable custom_id - was refused as a duplicate and never reached the component column. The probe registers, unregisters, registers the same id again (asserted back in the column's live list), registers a second id and replaces it.
The complete native-logic shape and width matrix.
Simulation state and level I/O mapping.
Enumerate and validate the pinned build's built-in component kinds.

The memory subsystem on a real board: the Symphony CPU's own starting board (two RAMs, six Load ports, four Store ports, zero wires) is deployed as the sandbox level, and the full raw component records from dev.sandbox-sim are checked against simcore's contract. RAM is 0 in/0 out, Load is 3/2 and Store is 5/1; every port's +0xe0/+0xe8 agrees on an 8/16/32-bit access, Load +0x88 matches that width while Store +0x88 is zero, the two RAMs report 8+0 and 8+16 address bits (256 B and 16 MiB), and both report big-endian mode at +0x178. The optional -CircuitPath can deploy a player's own saved circuit for the same probe.

tc.component.compose V1, the built-in type catalogue (M4's first cut): one entry per prototype the running build exposes, with the name the game carries, the stable spelling a Mod keys on (`builtin/<name>`, `#2` for a name this build repeats, `builtin/0x<kind>` for the slots the game leaves unnamed) and the declared pins. The probe checks lookups by kind, by exact spelling and case-folded, asserts the refusals (unknown kind, unknown spelling, pin past the end, bad direction, undersized struct) and dumps the catalogue. The playtest installs that probe next to the existing pin-table probe and runs both in ONE sandbox session, then requires the two independent readers of the prototype table - the SDK's TCGameModel wrapper and the loader's own get_prototype + pin decoding - to agree entry for entry on kind, name, pin counts and every reported pin offset and raw word size.
Basic plugin frame callback and ImGui rendering.
Drawing primitives, clipping and render-thread behavior.
Texture decoding, upload, ownership and GPU readback.
Prepare the shared two-plugin page sandbox through the common sandbox module.
Measure the real home-page entry rectangles for page drivers.
Prepare the page sandbox whose two plugins both drive their own page from inside the game.
Measure that sandbox's page-entry rectangle for the driver run.
Open and exercise a plugin page through its measured entry rectangle.
Two plugins with identical page and widget IDs stay isolated.
Measure the live board-panel hit boxes for the driver pass.
Board-panel input ownership, scrolling, collapse and scene lifecycle.
Measure the page entry used by the keyboard driver.
Physical keys, WM_CHAR and UTF-8 input in plugin UI.
Live level trace, board panel, VCD export and image evidence.
Per-cycle capture (TC_SERVICE_SIM_CAPTURE): the tick inside the compiled program fills a ring one row per cycle with no gaps, and the rows are the level's own inputs.
The scope board panel (local.scope): lanes resolved from the board's wires through tc.sim.channel, filled per cycle by tc.sim.capture with gaps = 0 while a real level runs.
A component with no inputs: the game imports the 0-in scaffold, keeps the driver whose input is unconnected, and calls the callback once per cycle.
A component with no outputs: the game keeps the extra driver node whose output is unconnected, and the callback runs once per cycle with the input it was given.

tc.component.types V2 plus the instance lifecycle: a nine-pin definition registers, the bridge binds it, TCLogicIOV2 delivers all nine inputs with the definition's own state size, and the probe walks the instance contract on the real build - enumerate, per-instance reset, storage write/read, delete and stale handles. Since 2026-09-28 it also asserts the placement half of TCComponentLifecycleV1: TC_LOGIC_COMPILE after a compile that contains the instance, TC_LOGIC_RESIZE (with the new half=3,2 read from TCLogicIOV2's placement tail) when tc.component.geometry V2 resizes that one instance, and TC_LOGIC_UNBIND when the probe leaves the board for another level. The move/rotate attempts are logged but not asserted: this build does not act on a synthetic board drag (see docs/research/component-hitbox-path.md).

A clocked definition on the full_adder board: exact visible dependency cones drive both outputs in REFRESH while a disconnected hidden sink runs the CYCLE callback exactly once per cycle. A state counter proves there is one tick, and the tick receives every input including the clock.
Board handle lifetime across a real level: issue, resolve, scene-change invalidation and a second level.
Board toolbar tool handoff and wire palette interaction.
The WordWatchee 64 package: shader text patch, live value_size ceiling and a board drawn by the patched engine.

Wide constants as runtime lookups: the player's own board compiles, a tape update costs microseconds and leaves the compile counter alone, and the circuit's own state holds the new value. Needs the saved profile (defaults to %APPDATA%\Turing Complete).
The other half of the generated-source dumps: with TC_MODLOADER_DUMP_SOURCE unset the same level compiles and the tape updates, and the game directory stays free of native-logic-source-*.txt.
Single-case component cost probe; the game tier uses the timing matrix wrapper.
Inspect one circuit fixture through the generic component probe.
Run one native-logic scenario; the game tier uses the full matrix wrapper.
Development probe for locating per-cycle level I/O traces.
Exact-callsite board-slot probe.
Toolbar font and framebuffer development probe.
Pin-label screenshot and overlap development probe.
Screenshot of a real board with every word label forced to 64 bits: the two-line low/high decimal layout.
Visible IME composition and candidate-window checklist; never selected by -Tier all.
Visible page demo; never selected by -Tier all.

The pin-order store behind TC_SERVICE_PIN_ORDER: cache reordering by key, contributed-bounds unioning, and frame geometry that uses a measured one-bit control height instead of cutting it at half-line height.
The pin-order Mod on a real level: the handles frame every entry of the left IO panel, a posted drag moves the entry it was dropped on, and the tc.pin_order service reports the new order.

The component catalogue behind TC_SERVICE_COMPONENT_REGISTRY: a declared type keeps its pins, costs and owner; the compiled shape overrides widths without losing declared names; a refusal is an inactive entry with the bridge's reason; unknown ids, bad indexes and malformed query structs are told apart; a rejected Mod takes its types with it.

M5 geometry/render consumer: the text box registers an 8x4 draggable footprint, keeps the game's own thumbnail/watermark off a board instance (pixel readback hidden=0 against an untouched visible control), proves such an instance is still grabbed and dragged one cell with the selection going 1 -> 0, validates rotations 0/1/2/3, live camera zoom and pan, and all four clip edges by framebuffer pixel readback, then completes its editor self-test.

tc.component.render V8 font resources, driven by the text-box consumer: the Mod loads the game's own faces through load_font (the CJK face with the full BMP ranges, the UI face with Latin), and the loader builds the atlas, uploads the GPU texture and owns the lifetime. Asserted on the real build: the service is reachable, both faces load with a handle/native size/revision, a relative path and an oversized range list are refused with ERR_ARGUMENT, re-loading a key without releasing keeps the handle and advances the revision to 2, while releasing and loading again is a fresh handle with revision 1, measure_font answers with face-specific metrics (CJK 42.6 vs UI 62.4 for the same text), and the drawing path itself has ink for the host default face (pixel readback). The loader-owned face's own pixels are still an open item and are reported, not asserted.
TC_SERVICE_COMPONENT_REGISTRY in a running game: a refused registration is listed with its reason and the bridged byte-adder component shows its declared pin names, widths and costs.

The sandbox simulator's own kernel (docs/PLAN-sandbox-simulator.md, S1/S2): four-state values with strength resolution, the layered time-wheel scheduler and its overflow heap, per-arc rising/falling delays, inertial and transport models, delta convergence, NBA, setup/hold, VCD/Verilog, explicit post-init feedback seeding, board constants, the game's auto-width Mux and Word Switch built at the width their record resolved, the Screen's latched settings and the pixels its documented modes describe, Time and Keyboard as host-driven sources, host clock runtime, and game-compatible RAM Load/Store ordering including held inputs across cycles - 255 assertions, no game involved.

The standalone simcore viewer's own layer (simcore/view): the board fixture format, the frozen pin geometry table, the cell-to-pixel mapping, click picking on components and wires, net-to-writeback-slot lookup, and the SVG writer - all of it platform independent and with no game involved. Also pins two semantics the picture depends on: a three-inverter ring oscillates instead of settling, and a cross-coupled NAND latch flips when its input pattern changes. The Mux fixture is a record a live session left behind, so a board a player built with a word Mux replays instead of being refused, and the Screen/Time/Keyboard geometry covers the peripherals the same sandbox board carries.

The external judge for the sandbox simulator (docs/PLAN-sandbox-simulator.md section 8.2): eight circuits - per-edge delays and inertial pulse filtering, multi-driver resolution including a weak driver against a strong one, Z/X gate inputs, a released three-stage ring, a 64-stage zero-delay chain, a D flip-flop shift register, a four-bit Maker/Splitter bus, and the game's four-bit word Mux with an unknown-select phase - are exported as Verilog, run under Icarus Verilog, and compared net by net with the engine's own event list. Skips with a printed reason when iverilog is not installed.

The sandbox simulator in a real session (docs/PLAN-sandbox-simulator.md, S2): dev.sandbox-sim binds a netlist to the running board - built from the component and wire records alone, with the game's own prototype table for pin geometry - runs simcore for each game cycle, and publishes its values into the exact state bytes the board reads (256/257, 258/259, 260/261 on the and_gate board). The report proves it bound, ran and published, and names the two-pins-in-one-cell cases it refused to guess. -Invert publishes the opposite value, which is how the suite proves the bytes carry the simulator's value rather than the game program's.

S2 off-path invariant: enabled=0 returns before resolving state or installing level, cycle, sim.do, or frame callbacks. The real session asserts zero behavioural hooks and no state report, so installing the package while disabled leaves game simulation ownership untouched.

The storage family on a real board (docs/research/simcore-kind-coverage.md, section 7): the Register (0x27), Counter (0x26) and Delay Line (0x37) declare no input pins in the prototype's own list, so the sandbox used to refuse any board carrying one with 'has no device in the library'. The board is written by tools/kind-fixture.py from the prototype table's hidden pin list, deployed as the sandbox level, and the case asserts the loader no longer refuses it and that the binding names all four devices (the constant source plus the three storage parts).

Custom components (kind 0x4E) on the player's own board, end to end: the sandbox used to refuse the board with 'component 7 has kind 0x4E with no pin geometry' (the type has seven outputs and the geometry table stopped at four). The case copies the player's sandbox architecture board and foundry definitions into an isolated profile, starts the game in the sandbox and asserts that the board binds - which now means the definitions were flattened: the custom prototype's own component and wire arrays (+0xe0/+0xe8 and +0x100/+0x108) are decoded, their internals become ordinary records moved far from the board's coordinates, and the instance's pins are bridged to the definition's boundary pins by index. See docs/research/custom-components.md.

Starting the sandbox automatically opens the simcore viewer shipped inside dev.sandbox-sim.mod. The real session requires the launched executable to come from this sandbox's extracted native package and to receive the live sandbox-sim-board.txt with --watch; the test then closes that exact viewer process.

S2 flagship: the closed three-NAND ring is built from board records without a game compile, keeps its three constant drivers, survives the game's failed-compile model reset, advances on the simulator-owned cycle, receives one explicit post-initialisation power-on seed, publishes into the board slots, and produces timed transitions exactly 3 stages * 8 ticks apart (48 ticks for a full value period). Since 2026-09-25 it also owns the state index of every wire (docs/PLAN-sandbox-simulator.md, 14.6), so the case fails if any net is still published to the shared placeholder byte below 256 or if the board's wire table changes shape mid-session.

S2 latch: a closed cross-coupled two-NAND board plus its three configured constants is built directly from sandbox records, advanced under the simulator-owned cycle, published to game slots, and required to settle to a stable known state for the final eight sampled cycles. Every net must also be published to an allocated slot (no placeholder byte below 256) and the wire table must keep its shape for the whole session.

S2 clock board: the registered host clock prototype is resolved by custom id, driven by the simulator-owned cycle, and its first NOT output must toggle one 8-tick gate delay after the clock while both values are published to the game slots - again to allocated slots only, with the wire table's shape checked for stability.

Sub-cycle publishing (docs/PLAN-sandbox-simulator.md, 14.7): the clock -> NOT -> AND edge detector produces a pulse one gate delay wide (measured: 1024 ticks of an 8192-tick cycle, i.e. one unit), far shorter than a cycle, so every per-cycle sample missed it. The case runs with one unit per gate and a sub-step of half a unit - a sample boundary then lands strictly inside every pulse - and requires the AND output to appear high in at least two published rows per rising edge (measured: 2 rows at half-unit steps, 4 rows in 4 cycles; the same board under the default cadence never publishes it). The report keeps four cycles of rows so the pulse cannot be truncated away.

Interactive switch (docs/PLAN-sandbox-simulator.md, 14.8): local.clock's SWIT_001 keeps its level in the host-owned instance configuration, and the game's generated program is what used to copy that level into a wire slot - suppressed in the sandbox, so the switch used to be frozen. The case writes the level the way a click does (instance config + refresh, exposed as the Mod's `interactive_level=` diagnostic) and requires the switch's net to be driven with it: level 1 -> net0=1/net1=0, level 0 -> net0=0/net1=1.

The clock's adjustable period through the game's own UI (examples/clock): the driver build of the Mod (dist/dev.clock-driver.mod) clicks the number box the drawing code registered in the component's corner, checks the value window opened for the clicked clock, types 8 and presses Enter, and then requires both the period the callback holds and the bytes the instance's configuration carries to be 8. The box-to-pixel identity (the rectangle the click handler hit-tests is the painted one) and the wave for each period are unit-tested in tests/clock-period.cpp.

Float Ops, package level (docs/PLAN-float-components.md, sections 4-6): builds the independent local.float-ops.mod and runs the offline tests first - the M1 binary32 kernel against 7571 golden vectors generated by an independent Python oracle (values and the five flags bit for bit, plus canonical NaN, non-sticky flags and per-thread SoftFloat state), the binary32 text layer against its own decimal vectors, the width text layer (named FP16/FP32/FP64 spellings, all 65536 binary16 patterns round-tripped, a binary64 sample round-tripped), and the compatibility test (five public V2 M0 probes, eight FP32 bit patterns through RESET/REFRESH/CYCLE, a missing tc.component.types service must fail the load, and the whole catalogue: 22 binary16 plus 22 binary32 plus 21 binary64 registrations - the binary64 FMA is deliberately absent because three 64-bit inputs exceed the loader's 128-bit input budget - each with its family's shape, pins of its own width, its own configuration layout and a callback that computes in that width). It then checks that the golden vectors are not stale, discovers, enables and disables the package in an isolated sandbox, and requires that nothing outside mods/ and tc-modloader-data/ was written.

Float Ops M0/M1 in the real game: 21 instances (source -> pass x17 -> result+flags -> sink, plus a Flags[5] sink fed from the dual probe's second output) bind as tokens 1..21 and every probe has to read the full 0xDEADBEEF pattern, with the five-bit output arriving as 0x0000001f. The plugin also has to report the M1 kernel self-check line (including a fused multiply-add whose result differs from mul-then-add), which proves the vendored SoftFloat kernel links into the shipped DLL and computes under the loader. A test-only driver takes the simulation over after the board is compiled and walks run -> pause -> RESET -> run, so the case requires refresh observations with the right values inside the pause window (the paused board still renders the pattern), the RESET summary to report zero mismatches, and the cycles after the RESET to carry the pattern again.

Float Ops M2 vertical slice in the real game (docs/PLAN-float-components.md, sections 6.1, 7 and 10.2): two FP32 Constants feed an FP32 Add whose R[32] drives an FP32 Display. The driver writes each instance's configuration through tc.component.storage - the same call the editors make - and reads the Display's own text back, so the case fails unless configuration reaches the instance, the kernel runs with that instance's rounding mode, and the result reaches the renderer: defaults show 2 0x40000000, 3.5+1.25 shows 4.75 0x40980000, and the halfway case 1.0+2^-25 shows 1 0x3F800000 under RNE but 1.0000001 0x3F800001 after the rounding box is set to RUP. The run also requires every service the editors need (render, geometry, storage, instances, ui, mouse) to be present.

Float Ops M0/M1 binding-token boundary: the same chain widened to 42 instances records where the loader's wide-output bridge stops working, with the M1 kernel self-check required in the same run. Tokens 1..32 must hold the pattern (a failure there is a real compatibility blocker); the measured result is that token 33 is the first token without a state slot of its own, so its consumer at token 34 reads 0. The per-token table is written to build/float-boundary-report.txt instead of being treated as a test failure, because the loader's documented limit is 32 tokens and expanding it is not part of this Mod.

Float Ops editor rows in the game's own component drawer, with real input (the player's report: 'the input box and the check box in the bottom panel do nothing'). The shipped package is the Mod under test; tests/float-panel-driver.cpp selects the FP32 Constant through the board's own select_component, walks the real cursor onto the drawer's label field and clicks it with real mouse messages, then types 'xy' with real keyboard messages and presses Enter. The Mod's own trace has to show the row window hovered with a live row (and the game's drawer not hovered at the same spot - that measurement is why the rows live in a Mod-owned window laid over the panel), the field has to commit ('the label field was committed after editing'), the instance has to carry the typed label, the board has to show name="xy", and no editor window may appear anywhere in the log.

The same drawer case on a board that carries more native components than a fixed handle buffer can hold (the player's report: '现在所有能写配置的元件都写入不了，都是写入元件配置失败。'). tests/float-fixture.cpp --crowd writes eighteen unwired FP32 Displays and *then* the M2 chain, so the constant this case edits sits far past the eight handles the Mod used to ask the host for. The host's tc.component.instances enumeration answers OK only when every instance fitted the caller's buffer, so that fixed array turned every write into 'the component is not on the board' - the label commit never landed. The case asserts the same evidence as the panel case (the row took the click, the typing and the commit, the label reached the instance and the board) and additionally that the log carries none of the write-failure diagnostics ('no live handle for instance', 'the host refused the configuration for instance', 'this write was not attempted'). Run against the shipped package it fails on the old code and passes with the Mod growing its buffer to the total the host reports - and it is the run that reproduced the player's own 22-component board.

The level lifetime a player walks through (the 2026-09-26 report: '常量的值还得我点一下才会刷新', '进入沙盒后退出再重进，会发现选中元件之后面板的相关配置不会渲染', '同 2 重进的时候，常量值输出变为默认'). tests/float-reentry-driver.cpp opens the level from the screen's own level block, edits one FP32 Constant's value through the drawer's 常量值 field with real mouse and keyboard input, leaves the level with the player's own Escape, presses the level entry again, and then selects the Constant *without touching a field*. The case asserts the whole sequence: the edit reached the instance's record; the loader's circuit save wrote the schematic directory the level's own meta names as its kind (schematics/architecture/Default for the level whose name is 'sandbox'); the second visit restored that record before anything was clicked (the display shows the first visit's value again with no click in between); and the drawer read the record back into its own fields (a later panel frame, the value row present, the field text equal to the saved value). Three rules only bite on this path: component ids repeat across a re-entry, so 'the instance changed' says nothing; the save used to write schematics/<level name>/Default, a directory the game never reads, which is why the Constant came back as its default; and the paused board's refresh needs the simulation model that the level load now hands the loader's control service. Run against the previous package the edit is refused, no circuit file is written, and the drawer never re-reads.

How close two float parts may be placed, and the case that drove both footprint fixes (the player's reports: '这些元件在垂直方向上 footprint 好像有点大了…不能贴在一起' and '其它元件都好了这四个还是有点问题'). tests/float-pitch-probe.cpp asks the game's own placement command to put a reference part and a second one one, two, three... cells below (and beside) it, each measurement in its own band of rows so an accepted part cannot decide the next answer, and reports the smallest accepted offset. Asserted: a stock-sized face (4.92 x 2.93 cells) reserves three cells vertically so two of them sit flush - subtract, the M2 constant, fma, split bits and make bits - while Compare keeps four because its four-output side spans rows 0..3; horizontally five face cells plus one cell for every pin outside the box (seven with input pins, six without). The two mistakes this guards: a half height the host rounds outwards (1.565 -> a four-cell box) and a face grown by a fixed margin (3.2 cells -> four). Fixing the four multi-pin types needed the offset-capable declaration (tc.component.geometry V3, set_footprint_cells), because the game lays a generated side out from row 0 and their faces therefore sit below the component's own cell.

Float Ops catalogue in the real game (docs/PLAN-float-components.md, sections 6.2, 6.3, 6.4.1 and 7.2): one instance of every binary32 catalogue type - Subtract, Multiply, Divide, Square Root, Negate, Absolute, Compare, Classify, FMA, Remainder, Round To Integral, MinimumNumber, MaximumNumber, I32/U32 To FP32, FP32 To I32/U32, Split Bits, Make Bits - placed by tests/float-fixture.cpp --catalogue with the M2 circuit beside it. The run asserts that the load reports the whole width cut (float-ops catalogue: 65 types registered, FP16 22, FP32 22, FP64 21), that each placed type is drawn with the stock 4.92-cell face (the multi-pin types taller, never narrower) and its stock symbol and name, that a type which rounds shows the five-mode rounding row in the game's own drawer while a type without a choice shows none, and that no window of the Mod's own appears. The binary16 and binary64 types register through the same table row with their own pin widths, so they are covered offline (tests/float-compat.cpp walks all 65 registrations and drives each width's callback, plus tests/float-text.cpp for their text) and by the palette case for their place in the menu tree.

The float types inside the game's own component column (the player asked for the folders to be part of the game's own category system, not a list the Mod draws): the game's palette builds its folders out of a custom prototype's name - add_to_menu_tree splits the name on '/' and walks the parts as parent categories - so the Mod names its types with a three-part path (its own root folder, then the format, then the operation's kind) and the game itself allocates and draws that tree. tests/float-menu-probe.cpp hooks the game's own reload_component_menu__presenterZutilities_u14192, waits for it to build the menu and dumps the tree the palette draws (build/menu.txt). The case asserts that the dump still has the game's five categories, that the Mod's root folder exists inside the custom category, that the root holds the FP16, FP32 and FP64 folders, that each of those holds the five kind folders (arithmetic, comparison, conversion, bit fields, constants and displays), that the subtree is exactly this Mod's 70 ids - 65 types plus the five M0 probes - and nothing else, and that no Float Ops id is listed anywhere else in the tree. docs/research/palette-categories.md records the measurement and why the tree lands inside the custom category (that is where the pinned build roots a custom prototype's menu path).

The width cut end to end in the real game (docs/PLAN-float-components.md, section 6.4.1), in three phases. Phase 1: the shipped package computes the same Constant -> Add -> Display chain in binary16, binary32 and binary64 on one board (tests/float-fixture.cpp --widths); the loader's own registration lines have to show the FP16 add with 16-bit pins and the FP64 add with 64-bit pins, and the Mod's own display lines have to show 1.0 + 1.0 in each format's text: '2 0x4000', '2 0x40000000' and '2 0x4000000000000000' (the hex digit count is the discriminating part - one binary32 formatter serving all three would print eight digits in every line), and the layout lines prove the new types are drawn with their own per-width value text. Phases 2 and 3 drive the drawer with real mouse and keyboard input (tests/float-panel-driver.cpp): the 值 row of an FP16 constant is the loader's width-aware decimal field (the declaration line reads value(float16), bits(uint), label(text)), typing '3.5' commits the binary16 pattern 0x4300 and the chain then shows 4.5 0x4480; the FP64 constant does the same with '2.5' and shows 3.5 0x400C000000000000. Before this round the loader's float row was four bytes of binary32, so those two types had only a hexadecimal row. The arithmetic, the rounding and the pin masking of each width are covered offline; this case is what only the real game can show - registration, pins, the compiled program, the callbacks, and the loader's own decimal field parsing a typed value into a 16- or 64-bit pattern.

Research case for the custom components' icons (docs/research/component-icons.md). tests/icon-probe.cpp hooks get_captured_path__presenterZio_u28 and the texture factory create_texture_unsafe/create_texture read-only and forwards every call unchanged, so the log names the exact file the game asks for as a component's picture: for a custom prototype it is '?snapshot_cc/com_custom_<decimal id>.png' under <game>/asset/ (e.g. com_custom_5058442071141929777.png for the Float Ops Constant), for a built-in '?snapshot/<kind name>.png'. The case clicks the component's body (the drawer's preview asks for the same texture) and then walks the palette's hover flyouts (category -> sub-category -> item list) while taking in-process GL screenshots, because the palette list only draws at the player's window size and only while the pointer rests on a level. Measured with it: a PNG dropped at the requested path IS read and re-encoded by the game, yet the run with the file and the run without it produce byte-identical palette frames (0 differing pixels) - the drawn picture is the game's own render of the prototype (design thumbnail + watermark: render_component_snapshots__main_u414, update_dirty_snapshots__main_u873, is_snapshot_mode__presenterZrendererZmulti95meshZmulti95mesh_u270). The probe also dumps built-in shape_svg fragments to show what a catalog thumbnail looks like for a built-in kind, and the companion run confirms that setting shape_svg on a custom prototype changes nothing (the same note is already in docs/PLAN-custom-components.md). Run with -NoIcon for the negative control.

tc.component.render V5 and V6 in the real game, on the surfaces that take a Mod component's own art: the item in the game's own component column and the preview picture in the bottom drawer (V5), plus the placement ghost that follows the cursor while a component is dragged out of the palette (V6). The loader answers the one texture request the game makes for that picture ('?snapshot_cc/com_custom_<decimal id>.png', once per frame) with a copy of the PNG the Mod registered, because a file dropped at the game's own path is read and re-encoded yet never shown (docs/research/component-icons.md). tests/icon-probe.cpp photographs each surface in-process (the palette's hover flyouts, a click on the component's body, drags out of the palette) and runs the Mod twice - with deliberately garish marker pictures and with no registration at all - asserting marker colour in the V5 surfaces of the first run and in neither of the control run's, while the ghost has to show Float Ops' purple body and pins in both runs and never leak the V5 marker picture. The probe now drags twice: once released over the palette (cancelled) and once dropped on the board (a real placement, which is the path the player reported), and both the cancelled cell and the drop cell are asserted to end up free of a leftover preview, with the loader's own 'taken over'/'ended' log lines required to pair up - a takeover that only ends on hide_clipboard leaves the successful placement's ghost behind, the bug this case was extended for. The pictures that ship (examples/float-ops/icons.cpp, generated from the Mod's own drawing code) are checked offline by the float-icons case.

The component pictures the Float Ops package ships: examples/float-ops/icons.cpp is built and run, and every one of the 65 PNGs (22 families across FP16/FP32/FP64, minus the FP64 FMA) is checked for the picture the board's own layout implies - a transparent 192x192 canvas, the purple body inside it (one cell is 26 px, so the face is 4.92 cells = 128 px wide and centred), the red pins reaching the +-3.2-cell lane, and enough white pixels for the width badge, the name and the symbol. This is the data half of tc.component.render V5: the real-game case (component-picture) proves the plumbing, this one proves the picture is really the part's board appearance at the board's own scale rather than a blank or a placeholder.

The rule behind tc.component.render V5 (src/picture_path.hpp): which texture request names a Mod component's picture. The accepted form is what a real board asked for - '.../asset/?snapshot_cc/com_custom_<decimal id>.png', with either separator - and everything else is forwarded untouched: the built-in '?snapshot/com_custom_7.png' branch, a missing id, bytes after '.png', an upper-case extension, a marker glued to another word, an id wider than 64 bits, and bytes past the passed length. Getting this rule wrong is how a picture substitution would quietly rewrite the wrong texture, so it is a case of its own rather than a comment.
